content:
Twelve hours a week went into cleaning spreadsheets nobody wanted to touch. I cut it to about two. Here’s the math, and the four prompts that did it.

6 min read
Just now

--

Press enter or click to view image in full size

The invoice that started this was $1,500 for a month of data cleanup.
Not analysis. Not modeling. Just taking exports from three systems that disagreed about everything — date formats, customer names, whether a blank cell meant zero or unknown — and making them agree.
A contractor did that work, monthly, for a year. That’s $18,000 for what amounts to reconciliation.
The uncomfortable part is that it was worth it. Nobody on the team wanted the job, and the analysis downstream was useless without it.
So I spent two weeks trying to automate it properly. Not with a scraper, not with a brittle Python script that breaks the moment a column gets renamed. With four prompts that handle the messy judgment calls a script can’t.
Here’s the honest breakdown, including where the math gets less impressive than the headline.
I share experiments like this every week in my free newsletter, AI Trends 24 on Substack. Join readers who get the real numbers before Medium does.
Quick Background: Why Data Cleaning Resists Automation
Everyone’s first instinct is a script. Write the transform once, run it forever.
That works right up until the source data changes shape. A vendor renames a column. Someone types “N/A” where they used to leave a blank. A date arrives as 03/04/2026 and nobody knows if that’s March or April.
Scripts don’t handle ambiguity. They either crash or, worse, silently produce wrong numbers.
That’s the actual cost center. Not the transformation — the judgment about what the messy value probably meant.
1. The Schema Reconciliation Prompt (The Three-Systems Problem)
The first job every time: figure out how three exports map onto each other.
You are a data engineer reconciling exports from multiple systems.Here are the column headers and 5 sample rows from each source:
[paste source A]
[paste source B]
[paste source C]1. Map which columns across sources represent the same field,
even when named differently.
2. Flag columns that look similar but are NOT the same thing.
3. For each mapped field, identify format conflicts (date formats,
name casing, currency, units, ID schemes).
4. Propose a single target schema, and for each field say which
source should win when they disagree, and why.Item 2 is the one that saves you. On my data it caught that one system’s “customer_id” was an internal database key while another’s was a billing account number. Similar names, completely different things. Merging on those would have quietly corrupted everything downstream.
Before: 3 hours mapping columns by hand. After: about 20 minutes reviewing a proposed map.
Best for: any merge across systems you didn’t build. Not worth it for: two exports from the same tool.
2. The Dirty Value Triage Prompt (The Judgment Calls)
This is where the money actually was.
You are cleaning a messy dataset column by column.Column name: [name]. What it should contain: [description].
Here are the 40 most common distinct values, with counts:
[paste value counts]1. Group these into: clean, fixable, ambiguous, and junk.
2. For every fixable value, give the exact corrected form.
3. For ambiguous values, tell me what it could mean and what
I'd need to check to decide. Do not guess.
4. Flag any value that suggests an upstream data entry problem
worth fixing at the source.That third instruction matters more than the rest combined. Without it, the model cheerfully assigns a best guess to everything, and you get a clean-looking dataset with invented values in it.
With it, I got a short list of genuinely ambiguous cases to decide myself. Usually 15 or 20 out of a few thousand rows.
Before: 4 hours of eyeballing distinct values. After: 30 minutes on the cases that actually needed a human.
Best for: free-text and categorical columns. Not worth it for: clean numeric data — use a script.
3. The Validation Rule Generator Prompt (Catching It Next Time)
Cleaning the same problem twice is the real waste.
You are writing data validation rules for a dataset that gets
re-imported monthly.Here's the cleaned schema: [paste]. Here are the problems I found
this month: [list them].1. Write a validation rule for each problem, in plain English
and as a pandas check.
2. Rank rules by severity: block the import, warn, or log only.
3. Suggest 3 checks for problems I have NOT hit yet but should
expect given this data's shape.
4. Flag any rule likely to produce false positives.Point 3 earned its place. It suggested a row-count sanity check comparing month over month, which caught a truncated export the following cycle — a file that looked fine but was missing the last 400 rows.
Before: problems rediscovered every month. After: caught at import.
Best for: any recurring pipeline. Not worth it for: one-off analyses.
4. The Cleanup Script Writer Prompt (Locking In the Work)
The last step converts decisions into something repeatable.
You are writing a production data cleaning script.Target schema: [paste]. Transformations decided: [list them].
Validation rules: [paste from prompt 3].Write a pandas script that:
1. Loads each source and applies the agreed column mapping.
2. Applies each cleaning transformation, with a comment stating
which decision it implements.
3. Runs validations and writes failures to a separate file
rather than dropping them silently.
4. Outputs a summary: rows in, rows out, rows quarantined, by reason.Never silently drop a row.That final line is the whole thing. The default failure mode of cleaning scripts is quiet data loss — 200 rows vanish and the summary statistics shift and nobody notices for a quarter.
Before: 5 hours writing and debugging. After: a working first draft in 45 minutes.
Best for: work you’ll repeat. Not worth it for: exploratory one-time cleanup.
Quick honest note: these four came out of a bigger system I’ve been building — 75 prompts covering the actual deliverables people pay freelancers and contractors for, not generic “clean my data” one-liners. The Claude Playbook is $27, roughly what that contractor charged for twenty minutes. If these four earned their keep, the other 71 will too.
The Math (Where the Headline Gets Less Impressive)
Time to be honest about the $18,000.
The contractor cost $1,500 a month, so $18,000 a year. That number is real, and it’s gone.
But “saved $18,000” implies zero replacement cost. Not true. Here’s the actual ledger.
The work still takes me about 2 hours a month instead of the 12 or so it used to take — reviewing the ambiguous cases, checking validation failures, approving the merge. At any reasonable valuation of that time, call it $200 to $400 a month.
API costs ran under $30 a month. Small, but not nothing.
So the honest figure is closer to $13,000 to $15,000 saved, not $18,000. Plus two weeks of setup time up front, which was real work.
Still the best return I’ve had on two weeks of effort. Just not the clean number a headline wants.
The Part Nobody Talks About
The savings didn’t come from AI cleaning data faster. It came from AI being willing to do a boring job carefully.
A contractor doing month eleven of identical reconciliation is not bringing fresh attention to row 4,000. Neither am I. That’s exactly where the silent errors creep in — the fatigue, not the difficulty.
The prompt doesn’t get bored on row 4,000. It applies the same standard to the last row as the first.
That’s a different advantage than speed, and it’s the one that actually compounds. My cleaned data is more consistent now than when a human was doing it full time, and consistency is what makes everything downstream trustworthy.
The judgment calls still need me. There are just far fewer of them reaching my desk.
Where to Start (If You Haven’t Already)
Take your worst column. The free-text one where every value is spelled four ways.
Run value_counts() on it, paste the top 40 into prompt 2, and read what comes back.
Ten minutes, and you’ll know whether the other three prompts are worth your afternoon.
A year from now, I think “data cleaning” stops being a line item on contractor invoices and becomes a review step someone does with coffee on Monday morning. The judgment stays valuable. The reconciliation doesn’t.
What’s the messiest dataset you’re avoiding right now? Drop it in the comments.
If this was useful, follow me. I publish weekly breakdowns of what’s actually moving in AI — not the press releases, the real stuff — at AI Trends 24.
